content.text:
Yes, I get it. Right now the storyboard is a script and the video is the product. You want the session to be the product. The system drives the real app through your test cases on its own, you can take over at any moment, and whatever you teach it gets written back into the cases. The video becomes one thing you can make from that.

You've already done a manual version of this: `eng-2131-canvas.checklist.ts` writes 11 test cases into Roam for the PR #1383 Loom.

**Core idea: replay what's known, reason about what isn't**
- Steps the test plan already has replay instantly, with no model involved.
- The model only works on three kinds of step: ones written in plain language, ones that broke, and things you just asked for.
- Whatever the model works out gets saved back into the plan as a concrete step, so the next run doesn't need it there. That's why a small fast model is enough.

**Two ways to steer**
- **Instant controls:** pause, step, speed, skip and pass/fail come from a small on-screen control panel in the page and go straight to the runner. No model is involved.
- **Plain language:** "open it from the sidebar instead" or "why are you doing that?" goes through the model in chat.

**Pieces**
1. **Plan:** test cases stored as data. Each case has an intent, optional steps and an expected result. Each step has a one-line reason. That reason is the control panel's label, the answer to "why", and later the video caption.
2. **Runner:** a version of `recordDemo.ts` that stays open for the whole session. It keeps the same launch, extension loading, actions and cursor. The scene loop becomes something you can pause: it can run on its own, go one step at a time, or stop between cases. It also gets a speed setting and a short wait after each step so you can follow along.
3. **Control channel:** the pattern from `interactiveDriver.ts`. It's a local Unix socket that accepts only a fixed list of commands, with no network port and no way to run arbitrary Node code. The commands move up a level, from mouse coordinates to steps like pause and skip. That file only lives in the eng-2152 worktree today, so it would move into dg-demo-videos. The control panel talks to the runner through Playwright's `exposeBinding`, so it needs no server at all.
4. **Model:** a Claude Code session running Haiku, guided by a skill. It waits for events from the runner and turns plain-language steps into actions by reading the page's accessibility tree. Playwright 1.61 can produce that as text, so no screenshots are needed. It also answers "why" and suggests pass/fail.
5. **Log:** every step, interruption, verdict and console error, with timestamps.
6. **Saving changes back:** the log becomes a proposed edit to the plan that you review in git. It's never applied automatically.

**Where the video fits: rehearsal, then the real take**
The finished plan turns into a storyboard, and the existing `recordDemo.ts` records the clean, narrated take from it. The current video pipeline stays as it is, so the first version needs no new video code.

**First version:**
- Roam only, on test-3-graph, with one plan.
- The control panel has auto, step and pause modes, a speed setting, and pass/fail buttons.
- Steering in chat, the log, the proposed plan edit and a session report.

**Later:** a chaptered video made straight from a rehearsal, model verdicts from screenshots, Obsidian and side-by-side runs, and voice control.

I'd treat starting a session as your explicit go-ahead to launch Roam, and point it only at test-3-graph.

**Two decisions for you**
1. **Where the model runs:** in a Claude Code session, or called by the runner through the API? A session needs no new setup and you steer where you already type. The API would respond faster but needs a key and more code. I'd start with the session.
2. **JS steps the model writes:** should read-only checks run on their own, with anything that writes to the graph asking you first? I'd say yes.

If this matches what you mean, I'll write up the architecture as a diagram and a decision log before writing any code.

A rehearsal you steer

Today the storyboard is the script and the video is the product. In a rehearsal, the session is the product. The runner drives the real app through a test plan on its own, you take over whenever you want, and what you teach it is saved back into the plan. The clean narrated take still comes from recordDemo.

  • Replay what's known, reason about what isn't. Steps that already have a do replay through recordDemo's runAction, with no model involved. A case with only an intent, a step that throws, or something you just asked for goes to the brain. It reads the page as an aria snapshot and answers with concrete steps. Steps that work get baked, so the next run doesn't need the model there.
  • Two lanes. HUD buttons reach the runner directly, so pause is instant. Language goes through the brain, which is where "do this instead" and "why are you doing that?" get handled.
  • Safe by construction. The socket takes a fixed list of commands, in a 0700 directory, with no TCP port and no Node-side eval, the interactiveDriver.ts pattern. Read-only commands (a Datalog query, an aria snapshot, element text) run freely. Any js the model writes waits for your Allow on the HUD, and the socket can't approve.
  • Every step says why. Each step carries a one-line reason. It's the HUD label while the step runs, the answer to "why are you doing this", and later the caption.
  • The rehearsal isn't the video. The session is filmed, so clips can come later, but the PR video is still a clean take: the baked plan compiles to a storyboard and recordDemo records it.

Sharing it

Two separate questions: how teammates get the tool, and what lands on the PR. A plugin answers the first, so GitHub only has to carry results.

Teammates install a plugin

Publish the runner and the brain's protocol as a Claude Code plugin in its own repo. A teammate installs it, points it at a PR's build and one of their Playwright Roam slots, and rehearses the PR themselves. Nothing changes in the discourse-graph repo, because the plugin uses the team's existing roamSession.ts and test accounts.

For that to work later, the rehearsal code keeps its own folder from day one and takes machine paths from flags and env, never from /mnt/data/projects.

Maybe later, if a PR needs more:

  • A commit status pinned to the head SHA, so a new push visibly drops the result. Your token can post statuses; check runs need a GitHub App.
  • A Playwright trace, so reviewers can step through a DOM snapshot of every action in trace.playwright.dev. The repo is public and attachments are readable without signing in, and traces carry network requests, so this needs header stripping and a secret scan first.
  • Reviewer replies on the report that become cases in the next rehearsal, once you approve them.

input.content:
# Live rehearsal

A rehearsal drives a test plan through the real app while you watch on
workspace 9 and steer. Steps the plan already knows replay through
recordDemo's `runAction` with no model involved. A case written only as an
intent, a step that fails, or something you ask for in chat goes to the
brain: a Claude Code session that reads the page and answers with concrete
steps. What works gets baked into a proposed plan, so the next run needs the
model less. The PR video is still a clean take from `recorder/recordDemo.ts`.

## Start one

1. Build and stage the PR's dist as the pr-video skill describes
   (`/mnt/data/projects/dg-test-eng-XXXX/`, whole dist, local DB env baked
   in when the demo needs it). Start local Supabase and
   `recorder/embed-stub.py` if the cases touch sync.
2. Run the runner from `discourse-graph/apps/roam`, in the background:

   ```bash
   npx tsx /mnt/data/projects/dg-demo-videos/rehearse/rehearse.ts \
     --plan /mnt/data/projects/dg-demo-videos/rehearse/plans/<plan>.json \
     --dist /mnt/data/projects/dg-test-eng-XXXX
   ```

   It opens Chromium headed on slot 3 (test-3-graph), loads the dist through
   Roam Depot developer mode, and prints `REHEARSE READY <socket>`. It
   refuses discourse-dev-graph unless you pass `--allow-dev-graph`. Other
   flags (`--mode`, `--speed`, `--dwell`, `--slot`, `--url`, `--no-cursor`,
   `--allow-login`) are listed in the header of `rehearse.ts`.
3. Open the brain: a separate Claude Code session, ideally on Haiku for
   speed, told to read this file and drive the rehearsal.

The session stays open after the last case, so you can add cases from chat.
It ends when you press Stop twice on the HUD or the brain sends `stop`.

## The HUD

A small panel in the page's bottom-right corner. It hides while a step runs,
so it never catches the test's clicks, and it sits in a closed shadow root
that page scripts and Playwright selectors can't reach.

- Pause or Resume, Next (run one step, or skip the hold after a step),
  − and + for speed (0.25× to 4×), and the mode (auto, step, case).
- ✓ Pass and ✗ Fail: give the verdict a case is waiting for, or end the
  current case early, for example when you spot a bug.
- Allow or Deny: the only way js the brain wrote can run.
- A note field: Enter files the note under the current case.
- Hotkeys: Ctrl+Alt+Space pauses or resumes, Ctrl+Alt+. runs the next step.

## Plans

A plan is JSON, because the runner writes it back. Storyboards stay
TypeScript for takes.

```json
{
  "name": "eng-2348",
  "title": "Stored Relations warning",
  "target": { "slot": "3", "dist": "/mnt/data/projects/dg-test-eng-2348" },
  "cases": [
    {
      "id": "share-warning",
      "title": "Share warns when Stored Relations is off",
      "intent": "Turn Stored Relations off, then open Share from the command palette.",
      "expect": { "text": "A warning names Stored Relations and says how to turn it on." }
    },
    {
      "id": "import-warning",
      "title": "Import warns too",
      "steps": [
        { "do": { "command_palette": "DG: Discover shared nodes" }, "why": "open import the way a user would" }
      ],
      "expect": { "js": "if (!document.body.innerText.includes('Stored Relations')) throw new Error('No warning.')" }
    }
  ]
}
```

- A case needs `steps`, an `intent`, or both. A case with only an intent waits
  for the brain.
- Every step has `do` (one recordDemo action) and a one-line `why`. The why
  is the HUD label and the answer when you ask what the run is doing.
- `expect.js` runs in the page; throwing fails the case. `expect.text` waits
  for your ✓ or ✗; the brain may propose one. With neither, a case passes when
  every step runs.
- `source` says who wrote a step: `plan`, `model` or `you`. js from `model` or
  `you` runs only after you allow it; `approved: true` is set once you have.
- `setup` (optional) is a step list that runs before the first case.

## The brain's loop

Talk to the runner with the control client. Every command takes one JSON
object, or `-` to read it from stdin:

```bash
CTL="npx tsx /mnt/data/projects/dg-demo-videos/rehearse/ctl.ts"
$CTL status
$CTL events '{"since":0,"waitMs":20000}'
$CTL steps - < /tmp/steps.json
```

Run it from `discourse-graph/apps/roam`, like the runner. Long-poll `events`
with the last `seq` you saw, act on what arrives, repeat:

| Event | What to do |
|---|---|
| `need-steps` | Read `intent`, `expect` and `aria` (the page as an aria snapshot). Send steps with `{"caseId":"...","steps":[...]}`. |
| `step-failed` | Read `error` and `aria`. Send a fix with `"how":"replace-failed"`, or `retry`, or `skip-step`, or ask sid. |
| `need-approval` | Tell sid what the js does and that it waits on the HUD. You can't approve it. |
| `need-verdict` | Optionally check with `aria`, `text` or `query`, then propose: `{"verdict":"pass","reason":"..."}`. Sid decides. |
| `case-end`, `plan-done` | Summarize briefly. After `plan-done`, ask whether to add cases or stop. |
| `session-end` | Report the paths the runner printed. |

When sid talks in chat:

- "pause", "faster", "slower", "next", "step mode": send `pause`,
  `speed {"speed":2}`, `next` or `mode {"mode":"step"}`.
- "do X instead": `pause`, write the steps, send them with
  `"how":"insert-next"` or `"replace-rest"` and `"by":"you"`, then `resume`.
- "why are you doing that?": `status` shows the current step's `why` and
  `source`. Answer from those.
- "also test X": `add-case` with `{"by":"you","case":{"title":"...","intent":"..."}}`.
- A remark worth keeping: `note` with `{"text":"...","by":"you"}`.

Writing steps:

- Prefer clicks, typing and the command palette over js. They're visible on
  screen, and they don't need sid's Allow.
- Selectors are Playwright selectors: `role=button[name="Share"]`,
  `text=Discover shared nodes`, or CSS. Pull names from the aria snapshot
  rather than guessing.
- Read-only commands run without asking: `aria` (optionally with a
  `selector`), `text` (a `selector`), `query` (a Datalog string for
  `roamAlphaAPI.q`), `screenshot`, `console`.
- Roam specifics from the engine README apply. Click a Blueprint checkbox's
  `.bp3-control-indicator`, not the input. Command palette labels must match
  exactly. Anchor title buttons with `:has-text(...)`.

Never point a rehearsal at discourse-dev-graph, kill the runner, or type
credentials. If the profile is logged out, stop and hand it to sid.

## What a session leaves

Everything lands in `output/rehearse/<plan>-<timestamp>/`:

- `journal.jsonl`: every event, written as it happens.
- `report.md`: the plan as a checklist with verdicts, what changed, notes and
  console errors. It's written as a PR comment; post it with
  `gh pr comment <n> --body-file report.md`.
- `plan.proposed.json`: the plan plus what the session learned. Review it
  with `diff -u <plan> plan.proposed.json` and move it over the plan if you
  want to keep it.
- `session.webm`: the footage, for clips later.
- Screenshots from `screenshot` steps and commands.

## Safety

- The control socket is a Unix socket in a 0700 directory with a fixed
  command list. There's no TCP port and no Node-side eval, the
  `interactiveDriver.ts` pattern.
- Only the HUD can approve js or give a final verdict, and it only accepts
  calls carrying the per-session nonce from the page's main frame.
- Steps from the socket can't `open` another origin, and `screenshot` names
  can't contain slashes.
